activities.anchor: Linguists formalise the contrast with Heinz Kloss's pair
activities.caption: file each case: structure, elaboration, or pure power
activities.name: socioKlossBuckets

config.prompt: Abstand or Ausbau — or is it just power drawing the line? File each case:
buckets: the line power draws, structure be damned

items.label: Serbian and Croatian — the textbook case: one speech community standardised into distinct national languages
Two varieties so structurally distant that nobody argues — separate from the start
Swedish, Norwegian and Danish — largely mutually intelligible, yet three languages (armies, literatures, states)
The 'Chinese dialects' — spoken forms mutually unintelligible, printed as dialects because they share a writing system and a state
A government deciding a variety is a 'dialect' — really deciding whose children must learn school in a second code

config.why: Abstand is uncontroversial structural distance; Ausbau is elaboration shaping one speech apart; and when neither fits, the decision is policy — one of the most consequential classifications in public life.

activities.anchor: no ranking of clarity or expressive range survives
activities.caption: find the line the standard-myth would love
activities.name: socioStdSpot

config.prompt: One line of this summary is the standard-myth speaking — click it:
lines: The standard is the variety of books and broadcasts, so it feels naturally better.
It congealed from a politically dominant region's speech through print, schooling and institutions.
Its speakers hold the good jobs, which is why it looks intrinsically superior.
Standard English won out because it is objectively clearer and richer than any dialect.
A language is a dialect with an army and a navy — the standard is the powerful dialect, not the better one.
config.correction: Nothing about the standard variety's structure makes it better — standardisation is a political process, not a merit contest.
config.why: The belief is understandable — the standard is the one in books — but no structural comparison favours it; prestige is assigned, then looks inherent.

activities.anchor: William Labov made the field quantitative
activities.caption: which curve matches the store gradient?
activities.name: socioRTrace

config.prompt: Three stores, three class tiers (S. Klein → Macy's → Saks). Which curve matches how /r/-pronunciation stratifies?
config.xlabel: store by class of clientele (Klein → Macy's → Saks)
config.why: About 62% at Saks, 51% at Macy's, 20% at S. Klein — a smooth social gradient, and within every store careful repetition raised /r/-pronunciation: social and stylistic stratification in one result.

activities.anchor: The strongest case is African American Vernacular English
activities.caption: pair each AAVE form with the grammar it encodes
activities.name: socioAaveMatch

config.prompt: Long stigmatised as 'broken' — pair each form with its rule:

pairs.right: habitual aspect — standard English needs an adverb ('she usually works') for this
copula deletion, grammatical exactly where 'she's' could contract, never where it could not
has been working a long time — fine-grained tense-aspect
a US court required the district to train teachers in the dialect's structure

config.why: Every feature is rule-governed: children's school difficulties come from a mismatch between home and school codes, not deficit — and every non-standard variety studied under the microscope has turned out to be a complete grammar.

activities.anchor: Peter Trudgill's Norwich study added the crucial twist
activities.caption: one speaker, two pulls — walk the rooms
activities.name: socioPrestigeBranch

config.root: You speak the local vernacular. Prestige points two ways at once — walk the week.

start.text: Monday: a job interview. The panel listens for polish. Which way does prestige pull?

choices.label: Shift toward the standard accent
choices.feedback: Overt prestige: the school-and-broadcast code pays here — jobs, authority, housing, courts.

choices.label: Keep the local working-class form
choices.feedback: Covert prestige buys belonging, not the job — and accent discrimination is documented in hiring with startling confidence and no accuracy.

overt.text: You got the callback. Saturday night, back among the mates from the estate:

choices.label: Drop back into the local form
choices.feedback: Now the local form carries toughness, authenticity, belonging — the self-reports ran the other way from production.

choices.label: Keep the interview voice all weekend
choices.feedback: The price of never shifting is distance from the people who know you.

cost.text: No local cachet cashes in here. Formal gates reward the standard — that is overt prestige, assigned through print, schooling and institutions.

choices.label: Now the Saturday night among old friends

covert.text: In the self-reports, men claimed less standard pronunciation than they produced — claiming more would read as betrayal. Which direction dominates depends on context.

choices.label: So what does one speaker actually run on?

distance.text: Accommodation theory names the fine grain: speakers converge toward (or diverge from) each other's speech to manage distance and identity — you have done this in every job interview.

end.text: Evaluations point two ways at once. 'Proper English' is the dialect of the powerful — useful, as any lingua franca is, but not more correct than any other complete grammar.

config.why: Overt prestige pays in formal gates; covert prestige pays in belonging — one speaker runs both, style-shifting by room, which is why style itself became a measuring instrument.

activities.caption: drag the divider across a diglossic day
activities.name: socioDiglossiaCompare

config.prompt: One language, two functionally specialised decks — drag the divider:

before.label: H — the high variety
before.text: Formal, written, learned in school: Classical/MSA for the sermon and the essay; Standard German in the Hamburg classroom. The Qurʾan's language sits at the top of the stack.

after.label: L — the low variety
after.text: Home and market: Egyptian or Moroccan colloquial; Swiss German among Zurich friends. Moving between the decks is a skilled register act, not confusion.

config.why: Code-switching obeys grammatical constraints — switches occur where the two grammars dovetail — and follows social logic: solidarity, topic, quotation, precision. Every human is plurilingual across registers.

activities.anchor: resistance to summer tourists written in phonetics
activities.caption: line up a change's life, earliest first
activities.name: socioChangeOrder

config.prompt: A change from below — order its life, earliest step first:
items: A variant catches on below conscious awareness, inside inner social groups
It spreads along dense, multiplex networks — street by street in Belfast
It rises to consciousness: overt comment, and possibly a change from above with overt prestige
config.why: Caught mid-flight on Martha's Vineyard, 1963: centralisation of /ay/ and /aw/ peaked among fishermen aged 31–45 with strong island identity — and Eckert's Belten High study showed speakers, not structures, are the agents of change.

activities.caption: true or false — reading the dialect map
activities.name: socioIsoglossJudge

statements.s: The Benrath line separates Low German maken from High German machen — the consonant shift, spreading north until it stopped.
statements.why: The textbook isogloss: a change frozen into geography.

statements.s: Isoglosses bundle cleanly, so 'dialect boundary' names a sharp edge.
statements.why: Variation bundles loosely, not cleanly — every boundary on a map is a simplification.

statements.s: Three lines fanning out at different depths is precisely how a change in progress looks on a map centuries later.
Where people think dialects begin tracks acoustics more than media and stereotypes.
statements.why: Perceptual dialectology finds the opposite — the audience's map rarely matches the isoglosses.

statements.s: R-fulness, the bath vowel and yod-retention in 'duke' all split the English-speaking map along one single line.
statements.why: Different features draw different lines — region, class and history are axes of the same variable, not one boundary.
